extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians (number theorists / arithmetic geometers) and mathematically literate public interested in the IUT/abc controversy
extracted.subtask_description: Discussion and informal standards for judging claims of major mathematical proofs (here: Mochizuki's IUT/abc claim) and the eligibility/assessment rules for a prize offered to demonstrate a flaw. Emphasizes publication/refereeing, explainability, expert checking, and possible formalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize decision authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Nobuo Kawakami makes his own judgment as an individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The donor (Nobuo Kawakami) will decide award(s) personally; the review method will not be disclosed. This places final authority with the funder rather than a public committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize submission / review eligibility (verbatim)
rubrics_metrics.description: The review method will not be disclosed, but the papers to be reviewed must be papers in mathematics that have been published on MathSciNet and have published more than 10 papers on arithmetic geometry in the past 10 years. Only papers that have been peer-reviewed and published in journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording on the prize announcement is ambiguous (it mixes references to papers and publication records). Interpreted conservatively: only work already peer-reviewed and published in journals and indexed on MathSciNet will be considered; the announcement also seems to set numerical publication/experience thresholds ("more than 10 papers on arithmetic geometry in the past 10 years"), though it's unclear whether that applies to submitters, reviewers, or criteria for selecting reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of peer-reviewed journal publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Only papers that have been peer-reviewed and published in journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be eligible for the prize (or to be considered authoritative), arguments should appear as peer-reviewed journal publications indexed in MathSciNet. Informal preprints or unpublished notes are treated as insufficient for this prize's stated eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on the claimant; conventional refereeing required
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof is on Mochizuki and anyone else claiming there is a proof, not on anyone else. The way to conclusively resolve this is to produce such a proof and have it carefully checked by experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valid resolution requires producing a complete, conventional proof that can be carefully refereed by experts in the field. The post repeatedly stresses that claimants must present a proof that others can read, check, and that will stand up to standard peer review; otherwise the community is justified in treating the conjecture as still open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explainability / defendability to other experts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no proof that anyone (Mochizuki himself included) can explain to anyone else; this is not about 'do I believe this guy or the other guy?'. Yes, most mathematicians don’t have the technical knowledge to evaluate this sort of proof, but there are plenty who do, and they are either saying there is no proof, or, for the few supporting the proof, unable to explain it to anyone else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A credible proof must be articulable and defensible to peers: experts should be able to state the argument clearly and answer questions. Lack of ability to explain the argument (or to respond to technical questions) undermines a claim of proof, even if the claimant is a respected figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalization as a verification route (with caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalization could be carried out since the argument was there, and allowed one to be sure there was not a subtle problem with the argument. That said, Mochizuki and those who claim that the argument is there could convince others by producing a formalized version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal, machine-checked proofs are an acceptable and strong route to verification, but typically formalization requires a clear conventional proof to start from. The Liquid Tensor Experiment is cited as an example where producing a detailed conventional proof enabled formal verification; without a conventional proof, formalization projects may not get off the ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial transparency and journal credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The source of the mess this subject is in is the lack of credibility in the way the IUT proof was handled by the RIMS journal editors. The editors of the RIMS journal that accepted the papers... have access to the referee reports, which either contain a convincing argument Scholze-Stix are wrong, or don’t. The fact that they have chosen to not release publicly such an argument and accept the damage to their reputation speaks volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For community trust, journals and editors should follow credible refereeing practices and, where controversies arise, be willing to provide transparency (e.g., referee reports) to justify publication decisions. Failure to do so undermines perceived validity of published claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise of reviewers / evaluators
rubrics_metrics.description: There are quite a few arithmetic geometers who understand well the problem with the proof... 'All negative public statements about the validity of IUT have been made by people who do not have proven expertise in anabelian geometry and who have zero research track record in anabelian geometry,' (quote from Ivan Fesenko). 'Fewer than 10 people in the world comprehend the concept,' (quote attributed to Fumiharu Kato).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should be performed by experts with demonstrated research track records in the relevant subfield (anabelian geometry/arithmetic geometry). The post reflects disagreement about who qualifies as an expert, and it highlights that perceived scarcity of deep experts complicates community assessment; nevertheless, the competence and track record of evaluators is an important criterion for credible judgment.
